song.title: Songbird
song.author: Mark and Helen Johnson
song.summary: We couldn’t have a spring collection without including the songbirds! Inspired one morning by a beautiful blackbird, this song seeks, verse by verse, to answer the question ‘What could the message be to his song?’ With its light and jazzy feel, we hope everyone will be encouraged to sing along.
song.teachingTips:
• This song has a fairly wide range, from bottom B to high D, so make sure you warm up the whole voice before singing it. Try ‘sirening’ from the bottom of the range to the top, starting on a low note. Repeat the exercise, starting a semitone higher each time. Then, remember to sing the whole song with a smile!
  • There are lots of syncopated rhythms throughout, so ensure the class can speak the words rhythmically before they sing them. Clap the pulse at the same time to highlight when the notes fall between beats e.g. ‘joyful sound’.
  • Focus on singing the wider interval leaps accurately and without swiping. For example, the perfect fi fths in the chorus on ‘joyful’ and ‘message’, and the minor sixth ‘of sun’ in verse 1 (and subsequent verses).

assembly.title: Super Seeds
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to look at the potential of seeds for new life and growth and also provides an opportunity to explore our own potential.

assembly.title: Light and Colour
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to open our eyes to the colours of springtime, talking about our favourite colours, noticing the extra daylight and appreciating nature's use of colour and light.

assembly.title: Extra Energy
assembly.description: What wakes you up in the morning? From birdsong to sprouting leaves and Easter eggs, this assembly helps us to celebrate all the energy of springtime.

assembly.title: Turning Over a New Leaf
assembly.description: This assembly looks at new leaves and growth in nature and helps us all to look within ourselves to see where we might want to ‘turn over a new leaf’ too.

assembly.title: People Who Care
assembly.description: The ideal assembly to help us to focus on, appreciate and celebrate all those who help and care for us.

assembly.title: The World Around
assembly.description: From the tallest trees, to the something you can only see with a microscope, this assembly encourages us to notice, appreciate and be thankful for the world around us.

assembly.title: Happy Endings
assembly.description: This assembly explores setbacks we might encounter in our lives and the characteristics needed to overcome them.

assembly.title: Feeling Hopeful
assembly.description: This assembly explores the meaning of hope and what it will take to realize our ambitions for the future.

assembly.title: Feeling Awake
assembly.description: This assembly uses The Parable of the Sower to reflect on what is needed to be ‘awake and ready for action’ in school.

assembly.title: Feeling Good
assembly.description: This assembly explores the uniqueness of human beings and how we can help others to feel more valuable.

resources.title: Brilliant Birdsong!
resources.content:
[{"key":"4e543859f25507b6","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To begin to define and recognize a range of timbres
  • To compose motifs using appropriate timbres and dynamics on instruments
  • To perform an improvised composition in an ensemble, communicating with fellow musicians
","title":"What’s achievable","image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"fd53ea199ac21aac","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Pitched and unpitched percussion instruments; imagination! 

","title":"What you need","image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"d0b892a7e077bab7","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

As a class, listen to some birdsong (www.british-birdsongs.uk is a great site to look at for this) and identify ones that you could simulate using percussion instruments or vocal sounds. (If you have any instrumentalists amongst you, see if they could use their instruments for this.) Focus particularly on the timbre, pitch and rhythms of the different bird calls.

Having chosen your birds, create a number of different birdsong motifs. Remember, you don’t need to copy each bird call, but use it as inspiration for your motif, e.g. you might choose a chaffi nch call and use a tambourine to tap at fi rst then shake, starting quietly, with a crescendo through the taps and diminuendo through the shake; or use a sand tube to create the call of a barn owl.

Once your motifs are created, work as a group to improvise a brilliant birdsong composition. Choose a ‘caller’ to start the piece by setting the scene. They can call out the weather, time of day, season and location, for example, ‘It’s a sunny morning in spring in the Yorkshire Dales.’

As you improvise, make sure you watch each other and visually communicate when someone should play next, join in, or sit out. You might want to select a leader for this, but working as a team is good too.

","title":"","background_color":""}},{"key":"64b46005cf05d9bf","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

The composer Olivier Messiaen was crazy about birdsong! He spent over four decades studying and notating it and composed numerous pieces using it as his inspiration. Réveil des Oiseaux (Dawn Chorus) is a piece for piano and orchestra that contains songs from 38 different French birds. Messiaen was a devout Roman Catholic and believed that birdsong was a direct link to the music of heaven.

","title":"Listen","image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"2829417441ee0606","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sgNeH9_8l0w","title":"Réveil des Oiseaux","background_color":""}}]
resources.summary: Use listening skills to define and recognize different timbres in birdsong and create musical motifs to stimulate these on percussion instruments. Then, work as a group to improvise a brilliant birdsong composition!

resources.title: Give Your Ears A Treat!
resources.content:
[{"key":"12eb209d59aaf6e9","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/SYHomepageImages/LandscapeImages/give-your-ears-a-treat-no-neg-1758553417AwlD3.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"3de4984da9a53614","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

A class of good listeners is every teacher’s dream. The good news is that, like most skills, listening can be developed with practice.  

Here are eight creative ways to explore the wonderful world of listening with your class: 

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"eac8c1b4b011a62e","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"1. Collect and copy! ","background_color":"#009CCF"}},{"key":"0d57486fde5fd5f9","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Good listening starts with the ability to discriminate one sound from another so why not simply have fun collecting, copying and exploring sounds? Sound Collectors or We’re Detectives are the perfect jumping off points for this, or take a look at Sounds, a wonderful onomatopoeic poem.  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"152fa910841dc0a9","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"2. Play with sounds ","background_color":"#D8127D"}},{"key":"41c63ebb5f51cf6d","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Have a dig around in the music cupboard and see how many different instruments you can find. If stocks are low, homemade sound-makers work well – just use everyday items such as plastic cups, wooden spoons and saucepans. Blow, Tap, Pluck, Shake is a great song to explore instrumental timbre and the music activity that accompanies the song What A Flexible Body! is a lovely introduction to matching sound to movement.   

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"3ac3a0de5179ff15","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"3. Nature sounds ","background_color":"#6FB843"}},{"key":"57e22f07aa2f46d0","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Encourage children to open their ears to the wonderful sounds in nature. Can they go for a walk in the school grounds and then create a listening map? What did they hear? Where did they hear it? If they walk to school, do they hear the same sounds every day? You might choose Songbird to explore the wonder of bird calls – how many different calls can they identify? Birds are experts at copying sounds – just take a look at this great example!

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"a2714055a1cd5550","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://youtu.be/mSB71jNq-yQ","title":"","active":false,"noMargin":false}},{"key":"ce717446d5cf9355","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"4. Group listening ","background_color":"#93699F"}},{"key":"1c015978338ca0d3","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Listening is a social skill and is something that can be practised as a whole class or in a small group. A good listening activity can help a class of children process and follow instructions, take turns, make decisions and cooperate and the great news is that all of this can be achieved with a musical game! Take a look at the Guess Who? music activity or try singing games such as Crossing The River or Marvellous Machine. There are also plenty of other games to choose from in My World: Singing Games.  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"1825cf33f36f1a2c","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"5. Listening routines ","background_color":"#F5BB26"}},{"key":"fee93a0b7ccfa20e","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Choose a song or a short poem and use it as your daily attention-grabber! Short of time? Try the poem, Shake It! – this one also helps children listen and control the volume of their voice – an important skill to master!  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"c3662931d3e83c23","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"6. Give your ears a treat! ","background_color":"#E15B64"}},{"key":"da31dda4041f63b2","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Everyone tires of hearing the same thing again and again, so try mixing things up a little. Providing a varied diet of listening choices in your classroom is a great way to develop your children’s tastes in music and also builds their understanding of people, cultures and the world around them. You could explore some of the listening choices in our music curriculum and why not build your own bank of creative listening choices to use in the classroom all year round – a great five-minute filler to get the class settled in the morning or after a busy playtime. 

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"d5cce4f3c3c587b3","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"7. What should we listen to? ","background_color":"#D166C7"}},{"key":"781e97a6ec9e01b8","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Songs like Don’t Go Listening To Lies and Keeper Of My Heart help us think about the messages we hear – positive and negative – and how we choose to respond. Ask the children about the sorts of positive messages they would like to hear through a school day.  

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"a671a212fbdbbe81","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"8. Just sing! ","background_color":"#15A881"}},{"key":"8620851b71d080f3","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Listening lies at the heart of all musical activity, so regular singing will boost children's listening skills. Try having them copy musical phrases or identify patterns in songs – Take 5 Styles  is a fantastic choice for this. Why not add a daily dose of singing to your classroom and see the positive impact it can have? 

 

Got a great idea for using Sparkyard to boost listening skills in your classroom? Please get in touch with your ideas!   

","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
